outcome: OpenAI's openai/math repository (public from 6 Oct 2026; paper folder dated 26 Sep 2026) claims a complete negative answer: for every real D, every connected component of the graph on Gaussian primes with steps at most D is finite with a uniform bound, so no infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes with bounded consecutive distances exists. The claim is Lean-formalised, is tagged 'research solved' in the formal-conjectures corpus, and is reported by Bloom (8 Oct 2026) as a claimed proof, but I found no public check by a mathematician; erdosproblems.com/952 as I could read it still shows the problem open. Every earlier event on this problem (computational moats, line and origin restricted results, a heuristic, and two withdrawn 'no' claims) is partial, restricted, or retracted.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one yes/no question with two parts. (a) Existence of an infinite sequence (x_n), n = 1, 2, 3, ..., of pairwise distinct Gaussian primes, meaning Gaussian integers that are prime (irreducible) in Z[i]. (b) Bounded consecutive differences: a single constant C with |x_{n+1} - x_n| <= C for all n, where the distance is the Euclidean distance in the complex plane (the statement names no metric; Euclidean is the reading used throughout the literature). The bullet fixes no starting prime, so it does not ask about walks from the origin or from 1+i (Gordon's origin variant, which the moat literature mostly studies); that variant is a restriction of the bullet, not the bullet. The statement asks for the existence of such a sequence, so a 'yes' would be a construction and a 'no' a proof that every bounded-step walk is finite.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's openai/math repository, public from 6 Oct 2026 (per Bloom's 8 Oct 2026 blog post and press coverage), contains preprints/Bounded-Step-Walks-on-Gaussian-Primes-September-26-2026/paper.pdf, titled 'Bounded-Step Walks on Gaussian Primes' and credited to OpenAI alone (per VibeMathed; I could not extract the PDF). The Lean scope note lean/docs/028.md states the result as: 'The formalized result gives a negative answer for every real step bound D'; 'one finite bound depending only on D limits the size of every connected component of the bounded-step graph'; 'Axis primes and all associates are included'; 'No explicit function of D is supplied'. The Lean target theorem (lean/OAI/NumberTheory/GaussianMoat/Main.lean) is fullMain : MainEndpoint ∧ UniformEndpoint, where MainEndpoint says there is no injective z : N -> GaussianInt of Irreducible elements with dist(z(t+1), z t) <= D for any real D, and UniformEndpoint says every component of the prime graph is finite with ncard <= B(D) and every finite injective chain of primes with steps <= D has length <= B(D). Bloom's 8 Oct 2026 blog lists problem 952 among 25 Erdős problems with claimed results and says: 'This PDF claims a proof of the following. Any walk on the Gaussian primes, in which the consecutive elements are at most D apart, has O_D(1) many elements.' and 'The proof has been formalised.' The formal-conjectures entry Erdos952.erdos_952 (lean file FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/952.lean) is tagged 'research solved' and its docstring says the problem 'was resolved in the negative, disproved by an internal OpenAI model in September 2026, citing [OAI26a]'.
events.revisions: The folder name, VibeMathed ('Solved 2026-09-26') and the formal-conjectures docstring ('September 2026') all date the work to 26 Sep 2026. The earliest public appearance I could confirm is the repository release on 6 Oct 2026, so I dated the event to that. I could not check the repository's commit history, so the true first public posting may be earlier. No version history was visible to me. The Lean scope note and Main.lean are at commit adc7f12 or later on main.
events.delivers: Under the Lean statements, for every real D and every starting Gaussian prime (axis primes included), there is a finite bound B(D) on the length of every injective walk of distinct Gaussian primes with consecutive distances at most D, and on the size of every connected component of the same graph. This establishes the negative answer to the bullet as stated: no infinite sequence with bounded consecutive differences exists. Restrictions: B(D) is non-explicit (the Lean scope note says so, and the catalogue describes the proof as a finite sieve over split primes leaving a periodic obstruction, using geometric sampling and entropy estimates); the result is over Z[i] with the Euclidean metric.
events.remains: On the paper's claim, nothing of problem_asks is left open: (a) and (b) are both answered. Not established: an explicit B(D), which the bullet does not ask for. Also not established by anyone outside the release: that the paper's argument is correct as written in its own TeX, since no human check of the argument was found (see checked_by and doubts).

events.directly_checkable: No single object. The claim is a theorem with a non-explicit bound. Checkable by reading the Lean statements (Main.lean fullMain, the Comparator target statement, and the scope note lean/docs/028.md) and by building the openai/math Lean project. I checked the statements myself: MainEndpoint is the negation of the bullet (injective, Irreducible in Z[i], Euclidean steps <= D), so the statement is faithful as I read it; that reading is mine, not a published audit.
events.doubts: (1) No mathematician has published a check of the argument that I could find as of 11 Oct 2026. Bloom's post says 'Bloom is careful to say that he hasn't yet looked seriously at any of the proofs' (as relayed by OfficeChai) and its own text says the proofs should be read as 'claims', not endorsed; for the 952 entry it says the Lean formalisation has not been confirmed to compile or to match the problem statement, as a general caveat. (2) The paper is unrefereed and part of a release of 719 manuscripts in 372 families (the count is disputed: 722 in some coverage), produced by one unreleased model under one procedure with about four thousand problems posed and about three hours of compute each. The README states that some unformalised results 'could have issues'; this result is formalised, which lowers but does not remove that concern. (3) The 'statement unaudited' flag from VibeMathed means no one has published a check that the Lean statement matches the bullet; my own reading agrees, but it is one reading. (4) I read 17 of the 41 Lean files; the rest are unread. (5) Earlier 'no' claims on this exact problem (Das 2019, withdrawn 2024; Stumpenhusen, Jan 2024, withdrawn) were withdrawn for errors in their arguments, though they used different methods. (6) The erdosproblems.com/952 page I could read (last edited 8 Apr 2026) lists 'Proof claims (0)' and no OpenAI entry, which conflicts with Bloom's 8 Oct blog; this is probably a stale cache, but I could not confirm it.
events.direction: Cuts toward the negative answer. The result shows no infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes with bounded consecutive distances exists, which is the answer the bullet's question is expected to have (Erdős wrote 'the answer is almost certainly negative', Er80 p.114, as quoted by erdosproblems.com/952). It does not assert the bound-or-existence question is trivially resolved; it proves a uniform bound that is stronger than the question asks.

events.what_happened: Kenta Kitamura (GitHub KitaKen1; Erdős forum profile KentaKitamura) posted 'Lean 4 proofs of a binary-form generalization of Erdős Problem 952 (Gaussian moat) and the all-degree binary-form moat classification'. Conjecture 3: for an irreducible homogeneous F in Z[X,Y] of degree at least two, a bounded-size component bound depending on F, D and r, with a complete Lean proof. Conjecture 4: for nonzero homogeneous F of positive degree, arbitrarily long injective bounded-step walks exist if and only if F = c(aX+bY)^m with c nonzero and (a,b) not (0,0), with a complete Lean proof. The README says Conjecture 4 'also resolves Conjectures 3, 2, and 1' and that the bounds 'rule out the infinite walk asked for in Erdős Problem 952' via F = X^2+Y^2 with r = 1. Conjecture 1 (the original moat question, attributed to Gordon and Motzkin) and Conjecture 2 (uniform bound, from OpenAI) are credited to OpenAI as 'solved'. On 10 Oct 2026 the same author opened formal-conjectures issue #7091 proposing three variants of Erdős 952 be registered 'research solved'.
events.revisions: The README records that on 2026-10-10 the author checked the single file on public Lean4Web. Repository commit dates are not visible (10 commits). Issue #7091 was opened 10 Oct 2026 and labelled 'new conjecture' the same day.
events.delivers: Analogue, not the bullet: a generalisation to homogeneous binary forms F in Z[X,Y] of degree at least two (Conjecture 3), and a classification of which forms admit arbitrarily long bounded-step injective walks (Conjecture 4). The author states that the Gaussian case, F = X^2+Y^2, follows and that Conjecture 4 implies the original question. I did not check that implication or the Lean proofs. Restriction: binary forms over Z; the bullet is about Z[i] with a single norm form.
events.remains: For the bullet itself, nothing new if OpenAI's result stands. The binary-form classification and its general-degree statements are the author's own, and their status is outside the bullet.

events.what_happened: Madhuparna Das, 'Walking through the Gaussian Primes', arXiv:1901.04549 (v1 14 Jan 2019). The abstract says the aim is to show 'primes are getting lesser as we are approaching infinity', with an algorithm to compute moats and a time-complexity comparison with Gethner-Wagon-Wick. A later comment (v3, 6 Sep 2024) says 'The claims made in Section 8 are incorrect because the argument is based on Cramér's probabilistic models, which are known to be false'. v3 is marked withdrawn.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jan 2019 (1,112 KB); v2 11 Apr 2019 (98 KB); v3 6 Sep 2024 (1 KB), withdrawn by Madhuparna Das ('This paper has been withdrawn by Madhuparna Das Ms.').
events.delivers: Its Section 8 bears on the bullet: as withdrawn, it relied on Cramér's model to argue for limited bounded-step walks. The abstract and the moat computations are about moats, not about infinite walks. I did not read Section 8 of v1 myself, so I cannot say exactly what it claimed. Restriction: heuristic probabilistic argument, retracted.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; nothing is established.
events.doubts: The withdrawal comment says the Section 8 argument depends on Cramér's model, which the comment describes as 'known to be false' after Granville's work. Withdrawn by the author.

withdrawn.what: v3 withdrawn: the claims in Section 8 are 'incorrect because the argument is based on Cramér's probabilistic models'

events.direction: Did not establish a result either way (withdrawn); if read as its author intended, it leaned toward no bounded-step walks.

The defined paths P_i (for i=1,2,3,...) do not cover all the Gaussian primes.', 'the paths include Gaussian integers, not just primes.', 'Without a proper error term computation, the claim does not hold'.

events.what_happened: Jordan and Rabung constructed 1, sqrt2, 2, sqrt8 and sqrt10 moats around the origin by computation. Sources date the work to 1969 or 1970 (the Erdős site says 1970, and the 'Gaussian moat' Wikipedia article's reference chain mentions 1969 and 1970). Secondary reports say that in 1970 they showed steps of length 4 would be required to walk from the origin to infinity. I did not open the original.
events.delivers: Moats around the origin of the stated widths. Restriction: origin-based, computational; a moat of width w blocks walks with steps below w from the origin's component, which does not decide whether an infinite bounded-step walk exists from another prime.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; the origin-only restriction leaves every other starting prime open.
events.directly_checkable: The moats are finite computations; the widths can be checked from the prime list, but I did not check them.
events.doubts: Year disputed (1969 vs 1970) across sources; I did not open the original.
events.direction: Partial evidence for the 'no' answer, restricted to walks from the origin.
events.object: Computational moats of widths 1, sqrt2, 2, sqrt8 and sqrt10 around the origin, as reported by secondary sources. Explicit (computed); not opened.

events.what_happened: Gethner and Stark, 'Periodic Gaussian moats', Experimental Mathematics vol. 6 issue 4 (1997). Secondary reports (a search summary of Wikipedia-like sources) say that starting anywhere in the complex plane with steps of length at most 2 one cannot reach infinity, and that the periodic moat method gives this for step sizes sqrt2 and 2. I did not open the paper (the PDF could not be extracted).
events.delivers: As reported: no infinite bounded-step walk from any start with steps at most 2 (and sqrt2). Restriction: specific step sizes, not all D; so it does not settle the bullet, which asks for some bound D.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for every D > 2 (or every D > sqrt2, as reported); the statement's 'there exists D' is untouched for those values.
events.doubts: Known only from secondary summaries; I did not open the paper.
events.direction: Partial evidence for the 'no' answer, restricted to specific steps.

events.what_happened: Gethner, Wagon and Wick, 'A Stroll Through the Gaussian Primes', American Mathematical Monthly 105(4), April 1998, pp. 327-337 (DOI 10.2307/2589708 per Wikipedia; 10.1080/00029890.1998.12004889 per another source). Secondary reports say it gives moats of width 4 and sqrt18, a computational proof of a sqrt26 moat (so steps of length at most sqrt26 cannot walk to infinity from the origin), and that no line in the complex plane admits a bounded-step walk to infinity through Gaussian primes. The paper won the MAA Chauvenet Prize. I did not open the paper (the MAA PDF returned 403).
events.delivers: As reported: origin moats of width 4, sqrt18, sqrt26; no-line result. Restrictions: origin-based moats; line-restricted walks. Neither settles walks from arbitrary starting primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, for arbitrary starting primes and all D beyond the reported steps.

events.what_happened: Ilan Vardi, 'Prime Percolation', Experimental Mathematics 7(3) (1998). A heuristic random model of Gaussian primes, modelled on Cramér's conjecture, gives a step-size threshold of sqrt(2 pi lambda_c log|z|) at a point z, where lambda_c is approximately 0.35 (a continuum percolation constant). Vardi conjectures this is the critical step size for Gaussian primes. Known from the abstract and secondary summaries; I did not open the paper.
events.delivers: A heuristic conjecture, not a result: under a random model, bounded-step unbounded walks exist above the threshold and not below. Restriction: random model; no proof about the actual primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; the model is not the primes.
events.doubts: Heuristic; the constants are from the abstract as reported in a search summary; the model's relation to the actual primes is the open part.
events.direction: Heuristic evidence toward 'no' (percolation picture), not a result.

I did not open the West-Sittinger paper; the report is from the 2020 summary.
events.delivers: Restricted: walks along lines in class-number-1 quadratic fields. Restriction: lines only, which excludes the general walk.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for walks not confined to a line.
events.doubts: Known only from a secondary citation; I did not find the original paper.

disputes.summary: erdosproblems.com/952, as I could read it (last edited 8 Apr 2026, 'Proof claims (0)', no OpenAI entry), shows the problem open. Bloom's 8 Oct 2026 blog lists 952 among 25 claimed results with a formalised proof, and the formal-conjectures entry erdos_952 is tagged 'research solved', disproved by an internal OpenAI model in September 2026. The two sources disagree; I read the erdosproblems page as a stale snapshot, not a decision, but I could not confirm its current state.

Origin of the problem: Wikipedia and erdosproblems.com credit Basil Gordon (1962, reportedly at the ICM in Stockholm, per one thesis); erdosproblems.com's blog says it 'likely originated with Gordon and Motzkin'; Erdős (Er77c) recalls it was 'told me by Motzkin at the Pasadena number theory meeting 1963 November' and 'apparently raised by Basil Gordon and Motzkin'. The erdosproblems page says the problem is 'not actually a problem of Erdős'.

Credit for a negative answer is split: OpenAI's repository credits the uniform theorem to the model; the KitaKen1 repository lists OpenAI as having solved Conjectures 1 and 2 (the original question and the uniform bound) while claiming its own Conjecture 4 'resolves' Conjectures 1 to 3. Both claim the bullet is answered; the second depends on the first's Conjecture 2.

summary: The one substantive event since 26 January 2024 is OpenAI's claimed complete negative answer, released in the openai/math repository on 6 October 2026 (the paper's folder is dated 26 September 2026). The paper, 'Bounded-Step Walks on Gaussian Primes', claims that for every real D every connected component of the graph on Gaussian primes with steps at most D is finite with a uniform bound, which excludes every infinite sequence of distinct Gaussian primes with bounded consecutive differences, including sequences through axis primes. I read the Lean scope note (lean/docs/028.md), the Comparator target statement (whose MainEndpoint is the negation of the bullet, as I read it), and the solution file Main.lean, whose theorem fullMain : MainEndpoint ∧ UniformEndpoint has no sorry in the fetched text. I also read 16 of the imported files, with no sorry, axiom, admit or native_decide in the text; the remaining 24 of 41 files were not read, and nothing was compiled by me. I did not read the 29-page paper itself: WebFetch could not extract the PDF, and I did not download it. The paper's own credit line and argument are therefore unverified by me. Human engagement: Thomas Bloom's 8 October blog lists problem 952 among 25 claimed results, reports the proof as formalised, and says he has not looked seriously at the proofs; VibeMathed reports a Comparator check with only the standard axioms, 'not refereed', and 'statement unaudited'. I found no public check by a mathematician. The AI attribution is repository-level: the README says the vast majority of results were obtained with 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model', and the Gaussian paper is not named in any sentence I read. Close calls: (a) Date. The folder name, the formal-conjectures docstring ('September 2026') and VibeMathed ('Solved 2026-09-26') all point to September, but the first public appearance I could confirm is the 6 October release, so I dated the event to that; the true first posting may be earlier. (b) Status. Under the Lean statements the result is a complete negative for the bullet, but the paper is unrefereed, one of 719 manuscripts in a release whose count is disputed, and its proof has been read by no one I could find, so it may be treated as claimed rather than settled. (c) The erdosproblems.com page I could read still shows the problem open with zero proof claims, which conflicts with Bloom's blog; I read this as a stale snapshot. The pre-window record contains no resolution. It has computational origin moats (Jordan-Rabung 1970; Gethner-Wagon-Wick 1998, width sqrt26; Gethner-Stark 1997 for steps at most 2; Tsuchimura 2004, width 6), a heuristic percolation model (Vardi 1998), restricted results (walks along lines, West-Sittinger 2017), and two withdrawn 'no' claims (Das, arXiv 2019, withdrawn 2024, for a, b nonzero; Stumpenhusen, 16 January 2024, withdrawn on 17 January 2024, for origin walks). Analogues (Z[sqrt2], imaginary quadratic fields, Eisenstein moats) are recorded as discarded events. A later binary-form generalisation by Kenta Kitamura (10 October 2026) is also an analogue; its AI use is disclosed, and its claim to recover the bullet depends on its own Conjecture 4, which I did not check. Note also that the Wikipedia article's footer shows a last-edited date of 10 October 2026, but the lead I read is unchanged and does not mention the OpenAI result.
competing_reading: The result could be read as not yet settled: a 29-page, unrefereed proof generated by one unreleased model, in a batch of hundreds of manuscripts, whose only checks are a Lean statement-level build and a formalisation-level Comparator run, with no human reading published by 11 October 2026 and the lead author of the release saying he has not looked seriously at the proofs. On that reading the status is 'claimed', and the problem stays open until humans check it. The stronger reading is that a Lean-checked proof of the exact negation of the bullet, with standard axioms only, is a complete resolution of the bullet, and the human-review gap is a matter of confidence rather than of what the result establishes. A narrower reading is that the bullet asks only about walks from a fixed start (Gordon's origin variant); the OpenAI theorem covers every start, so it covers that reading too. The AI call also has a competing reading: the repository-level sentence may not cover this specific paper, and the paper's own credit line (which I could not read) is what would settle it.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The 29-page paper's own text: its credit line (OpenAI alone, or a named human), its date, and whether it states that the model produced the argument. (2) A build of the openai/math Lean project, with axioms printed for fullMain and for every imported declaration, plus the remaining 24 files of the import chain checked for sorry. (3) An independent reading of the Lean statements against the bullet by a second person (I did one reading; VibeMathed flags the statement as unaudited). (4) A written check by a named mathematician, or a referee report or journal decision. (5) An update to erdosproblems.com/952 with a dated status, and to the Wikipedia lead. (6) The first public posting date of the paper, from repository history, to fix the event date.

incomplete: (1) The OpenAI paper itself was not read. WebFetch returns binary for the PDF, and the saved copies are outside the project directory, which CLAUDE.md forbids me to read. So the paper's credit line, date, and argument are unverified, and the 'OpenAI alone' attribution rests on VibeMathed. (2) The Lean project was not compiled. I read 17 of the 41 files in the import chain of Main.lean for sorry, axiom, admit, native_decide and unsafe in the fetched text, and the rest were not read; the sorry-free status depends on VibeMathed's reported axiom list. (3) The OpenAI README was read through the fetch tool's rendering for the AI sentence; the model names in the KitaKen1 disclosure ('GPT-6 Astra', 'GPT-6.1 sol') are as rendered and should be checked in the raw file. (4) Pre-2024 events from Gethner-Wagon-Wick, Gethner-Stark, Tsuchimura, Jordan-Rabung, Vardi, West-Sittinger, Miller et al., Prasad, Kinoshita and West (2014) are from secondary summaries; their opened flags are false. (5) I did not query arXiv search, zbMATH, MathSciNet, Google Scholar, Hacker News or Mastodon directly, so a 2026 claim outside the sources above could be missing. (6) The erdosproblems.com/952 page is a cached snapshot (last edited 8 Apr 2026) and may not show a later status. (7) The formal-conjectures issue #4981 (Aug 2026, a statement-formulation fix) is recorded in sources but not as an event, since it is not mathematical progress.
